def: An official document that lets you travel to other countries.
ex: I almost missed my flight because I left my passport at the hotel.
nat: You need a valid passport to enter most countries, so check the expiry date.

mis.bad: I need to do my passport in the embassy.
mis.good: I need to renew my passport at the embassy.
mis.why: "Do a passport" is not English; use renew, apply for, or get a passport.

def: The place at a border where officials check what you bring into a country.
ex: We waited in a long line at customs after the flight from Lisbon.
nat: The officer at customs asked me to open my suitcase and show my gifts.

mis.bad: I passed by the customs without problems.
mis.good: I went through customs without any problems.
mis.why: Use "go through customs" or "pass through customs"; "passed by" means going past something.

def: The act of leaving a place, especially at the start of a trip.
ex: The departure of our train was delayed by almost forty minutes because of the storm.
nat: Please arrive at the airport two hours before your departure time.

mis.bad: I will departure at 8 o'clock tomorrow.
mis.good: I will depart at 8 o'clock tomorrow.
mis.why: Departure is a noun; the verb is depart (or leave).

def: The act of reaching a place, especially at the end of a trip.
ex: On our arrival at the hotel, the staff gave us a cold drink.
nat: The arrival of the new manager changed the mood of the whole office.

mis.bad: At the arrival to the city, we took a taxi.
mis.good: On arrival in the city, we took a taxi.
mis.why: The noun arrival is followed by "in" or "at" a place, not "to"; "on arrival" is also common.

def: The suitcases and bags that you take with you when you travel.
ex: Our baggage was lost, so we spent the first day buying clothes.
nat: You can take one piece of hand baggage onto the plane for free.

mis.bad: I have three baggages to check in.
mis.good: I have three pieces of baggage to check in.
mis.why: Baggage is uncountable, so it has no plural; say "pieces of baggage" or "bags".

def: A cheap place to stay where travelers often share rooms.
ex: We stayed in a youth hostel in Prague and met people from many countries.
nat: The hostel was clean and cheap, but the dormitory was a bit noisy at night.

mis.bad: We slept in a hostel five stars.
mis.good: We slept in a five-star hotel.
mis.why: A hostel is a budget place and is never rated as five stars; the word you want is hotel.

def: A bag that you carry on your back, often used for travel or school.
ex: She packed everything she needed for two weeks into one small backpack.
nat: He carried a heavy backpack up the hill and was exhausted at the top.

mis.bad: I put my notebook inside of my backpack bag.
mis.good: I put my notebook inside my backpack.
mis.why: "Backpack" already means a bag, so "backpack bag" is redundant; also "inside" does not need "of".

def: A person who visits a place for pleasure and not to live or work.
ex: Thousands of tourists visit the old castle every summer, especially in August.
nat: As a tourist, you should always keep a copy of your documents with you.

mis.bad: In the city there are many tourisms in July.
mis.good: In the city there are many tourists in July.
mis.why: "Tourism" is the industry or activity; a person is a "tourist".

def: A famous building or place that is easy to recognize.
ex: The Christ the Redeemer statue is the most famous landmark in Rio de Janeiro.
nat: Use the church as a landmark, and turn left at the next corner.

mis.bad: We visited many touristic points in London.
mis.good: We visited many famous landmarks in London.
mis.why: "Touristic point" is a translation of "ponto turístico"; use landmark or sight.

def: A trip from one place to another, especially a long one.
ex: The journey from São Paulo to Salvador took us almost two days by bus.
nat: Have a safe journey, and send me a message when you arrive.

mis.bad: I will do a long journey next month.
mis.good: I will go on a long journey next month.
mis.why: Use "go on a journey" or "make a journey"; "do a journey" is not natural English.

def: A long trip by sea or through space.
ex: The explorers began their voyage across the Atlantic in the spring of 1492.
nat: The ship's first voyage to Antarctica took more than three weeks.

mis.bad: I did a voyage to Japan last year.
mis.good: I took a trip to Japan last year.
mis.why: Voyage is for long sea or space journeys, and we do not "do" a voyage; trip is the normal word.

def: A boat that regularly carries people and vehicles across a short stretch of water.
ex: We took the ferry from Niterói to Rio and enjoyed the view of the bay.
nat: The last ferry leaves at eleven, so we have to hurry.

mis.bad: We went to the island with a ferry.
mis.good: We went to the island by ferry.
mis.why: Use "by + transport" without an article, or "on the ferry"; "with a ferry" is wrong.

def: The raised area beside a railway track where passengers wait for trains.
ex: The train to Berlin will leave from platform nine in ten minutes.
nat: Please stand behind the yellow line on the platform until the train stops.

mis.bad: The train arrives in the platform four.
mis.good: The train arrives at platform four.
mis.why: Use "at platform four" with no article; "in the platform" is wrong.

def: A list showing the times when buses, trains, or classes happen.
ex: The bus timetable changes in winter, so check it before you plan your trip.
nat: According to the timetable, the next train to Leeds leaves at half past four.

mis.bad: The timetable say the bus leaves at five.
mis.good: The timetable says the bus leaves at five.
mis.why: A singular subject needs "says".

def: A track with two metal rails on which trains travel.
ex: The old railway through the mountains is now a popular route for tourists.
nat: They are building a new railway to connect the port with the capital.

mis.bad: I live near of the railway station.
mis.good: I live near the railway station.
mis.why: "Near" is followed directly by the noun, with no "of".

def: A wide road for fast traffic, with several lanes in each direction.
ex: We drove for three hours on the motorway before stopping for coffee.
nat: There was a serious accident on the motorway, so traffic stopped completely.

mis.bad: We drive in the motorway every day to work.
mis.good: We drive on the motorway every day to work.
mis.why: We drive "on" a motorway, not "in" it.

def: A situation where too many vehicles or people are in one place and cannot move easily.
ex: Heavy congestion in the city center makes the morning commute much longer.
nat: The new toll should reduce congestion on the main roads during rush hour.

mis.bad: There is a big congestion on the road.
mis.good: There is heavy congestion on the road.
mis.why: Congestion is uncountable, so it cannot take "a"; also "heavy" collocates better than "big".

def: A circular road junction where vehicles drive around a central island.
ex: Take the second exit at the roundabout, and the museum will be on your left.
nat: There is a small roundabout at the end of our street.

mis.bad: Turn on the roundabout and go straight.
mis.good: Go to the roundabout and take the second exit.
mis.why: You cannot "turn on" a roundabout; you take an exit at or from it.

def: A longer route that you take to avoid a problem or to visit a place.
ex: We made a detour through the village to avoid the road works.
nat: Because of the flood, we had to take a long detour to reach the airport.

mis.bad: We made a deviation to see the lake.
mis.good: We made a detour to see the lake.
mis.why: "Deviation" is not used for a change of route in travel; the word is detour.

def: To travel by getting free rides from passing cars.
ex: When I was a student, I hitchhiked across Europe with my best friend.
nat: It is not safe to hitchhike alone at night, so travel with a friend.

mis.bad: We went hitchhike to the coast last summer.
mis.good: We went hitchhiking to the coast last summer.
mis.why: After "go" for activities, use the -ing form: go hitchhiking.

pt: pessoa que viaja diariamente para o trabalho
def: A person who travels regularly between home and work.
ex: Thousands of commuters were stuck at the station because of the strike.
nat: Most commuters in this town take the early train to the capital.

mis.bad: The commuters are people who go to travel on holidays.
mis.good: Commuters are people who travel to work every day.
mis.why: A commuter travels regularly to work, not on holiday; holidaymakers or tourists go on holidays.

def: A person who travels in a vehicle but does not drive it or work on it.
ex: All passengers must keep their seat belts fastened during take-off and landing.
nat: The bus was almost empty, with only three passengers on board.

mis.bad: The bus has place for fifty passengers.
mis.good: The bus has room for fifty passengers.
mis.why: "Place" is not used for space in this sense; use "room" (uncountable) or "seats".

def: A holiday on a large ship that visits several places.
ex: They went on a cruise around the Greek islands for their anniversary.
nat: The cruise ship stops at three ports during the week-long trip.

mis.bad: We did a cruise in the Mediterranean last summer.
mis.good: We went on a cruise in the Mediterranean last summer.
mis.why: Use "go on a cruise" or "take a cruise"; "do a cruise" is not natural.

def: An official stamp or document that allows you to enter or stay in a country.
ex: She applied for a work visa three months before moving to Canada.
nat: You do not need a visa to stay for less than ninety days.

mis.bad: I did the visa in the consulate.
mis.good: I applied for a visa at the consulate.
mis.why: "Do a visa" is a literal translation; use "apply for" or "get" a visa.

def: To go onto a ship or plane, or to begin a new project.
ex: The passengers embarked at noon and the ship left the port an hour later.
nat: After finishing college, she embarked on a career in journalism.

mis.bad: He embarked in a new business last year.
mis.good: He embarked on a new business last year.
mis.why: The verb takes "on" for beginning a project; "embark in" is wrong.

def: Sudden movements of air that make a plane shake during a flight.
ex: We hit some turbulence over the mountains, and the captain asked everyone to sit down.
nat: Light turbulence is normal and does not mean the plane is in danger.

mis.bad: The plane had a lot of turbulences.
mis.good: The plane had a lot of turbulence.
mis.why: Turbulence is uncountable and has no plural form here.

def: A long strip of ground where planes take off and land.
ex: The plane waited on the runway for twenty minutes before it could take off.
nat: Heavy fog closed the runway and all flights were delayed.

mis.bad: The plane landed in the runway of the airport.
mis.good: The plane landed on the runway of the airport.
mis.why: Planes land "on" the runway, not "in" it.

pt: veículo de translado, ônibus de ligação
def: A bus, train, or plane that goes regularly between two places.
ex: A free shuttle takes guests from the hotel to the airport every thirty minutes.
nat: We missed the airport shuttle, so we had to take an expensive taxi.

mis.bad: The hotel offers a shuttle to the airport by free.
mis.good: The hotel offers a free shuttle to the airport.
mis.why: Free is an adjective placed before the noun; "by free" is wrong.

def: The path at the side of a road where people walk.
ex: Please do not ride your bike on the pavement because it is dangerous for walkers.
nat: The pavement was wet and slippery after the rain.

mis.bad: I walked in the pavement because there was no street.
mis.good: I walked on the pavement because there was no road.
mis.why: We walk "on" the pavement, not "in" it.

def: A set of rooms for living in, on one floor of a larger building.
ex: They bought a small apartment near the beach and moved in last month.
nat: Our apartment is on the fifth floor, and the elevator is often broken.

mis.bad: I live in a apartment with two bedrooms.
mis.good: I live in an apartment with two bedrooms.
mis.why: Use "an" before a vowel sound; apartment starts with a vowel sound.

def: A person who shares an apartment with you but is not your family.
ex: My flatmate is very tidy, so our kitchen is always clean.
nat: I am looking for a new flatmate because mine is moving to another city.

mis.bad: I live with a colleague of apartment.
mis.good: I live with a flatmate.
mis.why: "Colleague of apartment" is a literal translation; the word is flatmate or roommate.

def: A legal agreement to rent a house or property for a fixed period.
ex: We signed a one-year lease for the apartment and paid the first month.
nat: The lease ends in June, so we must decide whether to renew it.

mis.bad: I signed the lease of rent for one year.
mis.good: I signed a one-year lease.
mis.why: "Lease of rent" is redundant; say "a one-year lease".

def: Basic services like electricity, water, and gas used in a home.
ex: The rent includes all utilities, so we do not receive separate bills.
nat: Utilities are expensive in winter because of the heating.

mis.bad: The utility is included in the rent.
mis.good: The utilities are included in the rent.
mis.why: Use the plural utilities for water, gas, and electricity.

def: A small platform with a wall or rail outside an upper window or door.
ex: We had breakfast on the balcony and watched the sun rise over the sea.
nat: Our apartment has a small balcony where I grow herbs.

mis.bad: I like to sit in the balcony in the evening.
mis.good: I like to sit on the balcony in the evening.
mis.why: We sit "on" a balcony, not "in" it.

def: A room or floor of a building that is partly or fully below ground level.
ex: Water came into the basement during the storm and damaged our boxes.
nat: They turned the basement into a small gym with a few machines.

mis.bad: We keep the bikes on the basement.
mis.good: We keep the bikes in the basement.
mis.why: Use "in" for a room below ground.

def: A space under the roof of a house, often used for storing things.
ex: I found my old school photos in a box in the attic.
nat: The attic gets very hot in summer because it is just under the roof.

mis.bad: My toys are in the garret of the house.
mis.good: My toys are in the attic.
mis.why: Garret is an old, rare word; the normal word is attic.

def: The inner surface at the top of a room, above your head.
ex: There is a big crack in the ceiling above the kitchen table.
nat: The room has a high ceiling, so it feels bright and spacious.

mis.bad: The paint of the roof inside is falling.
mis.good: The paint on the ceiling is falling off.
mis.why: "Roof" is the outside top of a building; the inside surface is the ceiling.

def: A set of steps going from one level of a building to another.
ex: The old house has a beautiful wooden staircase in the entrance hall.
nat: Take the staircase if the elevator is full.

mis.bad: I went up by the stairs of the staircase.
mis.good: I went up the staircase.
mis.why: "Stairs of the staircase" is redundant; say "went up the staircase" or "took the stairs".

def: A structure around a garden or field, usually made of wood or metal.
ex: The neighbors painted the fence white and planted flowers next to it.
nat: Our dog jumped over the fence and ran into the street.

mis.bad: I built a wall of wood around my garden.
mis.good: I built a wooden fence around my garden.
mis.why: A fence is the light barrier made of wood or wire; a wall is usually stone or brick, so "wall of wood" sounds wrong.

def: An area of ground next to a house, often with grass.
ex: The children play football in the yard every afternoon after school.
nat: We are planning to build a small pool in the back yard.

mis.bad: I have a garden of vegetables in my house back.
mis.good: I have a vegetable garden in my back yard.
mis.why: Word order and "of" are wrong here; "back yard" is the area behind the house.

def: A button by the door that makes a sound inside when you press it.
ex: The doorbell rang while I was in the shower, so I did not answer.
nat: Please ring the doorbell twice, because the sound is very quiet.

mis.bad: I touched the bell of the door to call someone.
mis.good: I rang the doorbell.
mis.why: The natural verb is "ring" the doorbell; "bell of the door" is a literal translation.

def: A piece of cloth that hangs in front of a window or door.
ex: She closed the curtains because the afternoon sun was too bright.
nat: The curtain went up, and the audience stopped talking.

mis.bad: I opened the courtain to see the sun.
mis.good: I opened the curtains to see the sun.
mis.why: The spelling is curtain, and it is normally plural for windows.

def: A soft bag that you put on a chair or sofa to make it more comfortable.
ex: He put a cushion behind his back because the chair was hard.
nat: The sofa has four colorful cushions that match the walls.

mis.bad: I sleep with a cushion under my head every night.
mis.good: I sleep with a pillow under my head every night.
mis.why: A cushion is for sofas and chairs; for sleeping, the word is pillow.

def: A tall cupboard where you hang your clothes.
ex: My wardrobe is so full that I cannot close the doors.
nat: She bought a new wardrobe for the bedroom, but it was difficult to build.

mis.bad: My wardrobe have too many old shirts.
mis.good: My wardrobe has too many old shirts.
mis.why: A singular noun takes "has", not "have".

def: A flat board fixed to a wall or in a cupboard for putting things on.
ex: I put the books on the top shelf, where the children cannot reach them.
nat: There are several shelves in the kitchen for plates and glasses.

mis.bad: I have many books in the shelfs.
mis.good: I have many books on the shelves.
mis.why: The plural of shelf is shelves, and we say "on the shelves".

def: A part of a desk or cabinet that you pull out to put things in.
ex: I keep my passport in the top drawer of my desk.
nat: She opened the drawer and found the keys she had lost last week.

mis.bad: I keep my keys in the draw.
mis.good: I keep my keys in the drawer.
mis.why: The furniture part is spelled and pronounced drawer; "draw" is the verb for making pictures.

def: A person whose job is to fit and repair water pipes and bathrooms.
ex: We called a plumber because water was dripping from the kitchen sink.
nat: The plumber fixed the leak in less than an hour and charged us fifty pounds.

mis.bad: The plumber arrived and fix the sink quickly.
mis.good: The plumber arrived and fixed the sink quickly.
mis.why: The second verb must also be in the past tense: arrived and fixed.

def: A hole or crack where liquid or gas escapes, or the escaping itself.
ex: There is a leak in the roof, and water drips into the bucket every night.
nat: The company found a gas leak and evacuated the whole building.

mis.bad: The pipe is leaking water of the roof.
mis.good: The pipe is leaking water from the roof.
mis.why: The water comes "from" the roof, not "of" the roof.

def: Material that stops heat or sound from passing through walls or roofs.
ex: Good insulation can reduce your heating bill by more than twenty percent.
nat: The old house has poor insulation, so it feels freezing in winter.

mis.bad: The house has a bad isolation and is very cold.
mis.good: The house has poor insulation and is very cold.
mis.why: "Isolation" means being alone; for heat or sound the word is insulation.

def: To move to a new place to live or work.
ex: Her company relocated her to Madrid, so she sold her car and left.
nat: We may relocate to a smaller town to enjoy a quieter life.

mis.bad: They relocated for another city last year.
mis.good: They relocated to another city last year.
mis.why: Relocate takes "to" before the destination, not "for".

def: Having a lot of space inside, so that it feels large and comfortable.
ex: The hotel room was spacious and had a large window facing the sea.
nat: We are looking for a more spacious apartment with a separate study.

mis.bad: The house is very spacey and has big rooms.
mis.good: The house is very spacious and has big rooms.
mis.why: "Spacey" means dreamy or distracted; the adjective for large rooms is spacious.

def: Too small, with not enough room to move comfortably.
ex: Five people lived in a cramped apartment with only one bedroom.
nat: The seats on the bus were so cramped that I could not stretch my legs.

mis.bad: The room was too much tight for four people.
mis.good: The room was too cramped for four people.
mis.why: "Too much tight" is wrong; use "too cramped" or "too small".

def: Warm, comfortable, and pleasant, especially in a small place.
ex: We spent a cozy evening by the fire, drinking tea and reading.
nat: The little café was cozy, with soft lights and old wooden tables.

mis.bad: The room was cozy, we felt very comfortably.
mis.good: The room was cozy, so we felt very comfortable.
mis.why: After "feel", use the adjective comfortable, not the adverb comfortably.

def: Empty and not being used by anyone.
ex: There are no vacant rooms at the hotel because of the music festival.
nat: The office on the second floor has been vacant for six months.

mis.bad: The seat was vague, so I sat there.
mis.good: The seat was vacant, so I sat there.
mis.why: "Vague" means unclear; for an empty seat, use vacant.

def: A lot of things in an untidy mess, filling a space.
ex: The desk was covered in clutter, so I could not find my keys.
nat: I hate clutter, so I give away things I do not use.

mis.bad: The room has many clutters on the floor.
mis.good: The room has a lot of clutter on the floor.
mis.why: Clutter is uncountable, so it has no plural and no "many".

def: To remove things you do not need from a place to make it tidy.
ex: We decluttered the garage last weekend and gave six boxes to charity.
nat: If you declutter your desk, you will probably work better.

mis.bad: I decluttered the house for old things.
mis.good: I decluttered the house by throwing away old things.
mis.why: Use "by + -ing" to say how you did it; "for old things" changes the meaning.

def: The step in front of a door, or the area just outside it.
ex: A package was waiting on the doorstep when I got home from work.
nat: They have a lovely beach right on their doorstep.

mis.bad: The delivery man left the box in the doorstep.
mis.good: The delivery man left the box on the doorstep.
mis.why: We say "on the doorstep", not "in the doorstep".

def: To cut grass with a machine.
ex: My father mows the lawn every Saturday morning before it gets hot.
nat: I need to mow the grass before the rain starts.

mis.bad: My father mow the lawn every Saturday.
mis.good: My father mows the lawn every Saturday.
mis.why: Third person singular present needs -s: he mows.

def: A place in a wall of a room where you can burn wood to heat the room.
ex: We sat by the fireplace and talked until the wood burned out.
nat: The cottage has a stone fireplace in the living room.

mis.bad: We put the wood in the chimney to heat the room.
mis.good: We put the wood in the fireplace to heat the room.
mis.why: The chimney is the pipe on the roof; the wood goes in the fireplace.

def: The business of selling goods directly to customers in shops or online.
ex: She works in retail, so she is very busy before Christmas.
nat: Retail sales rose by five percent in the last quarter.

mis.bad: She works in the retail of clothes.
mis.good: She works in clothing retail.
mis.why: Retail is used as an uncountable noun without "the" and "of"; use a noun adjunct like "clothing retail".

def: A metal cart that you push around a supermarket to carry your shopping.
ex: I put the milk and the eggs in the trolley and went to the checkout.
nat: Someone left a trolley in the middle of the parking lot.

mis.bad: I put the products in the car of the market.
mis.good: I put the groceries in the trolley.
mis.why: "Car of the market" is a literal translation; a supermarket cart is a trolley.

def: A narrow path between rows of shelves in a shop, or between seats.
ex: The cereal is in aisle five, next to the coffee and tea.
nat: I always ask for an aisle seat so I can stand up easily.

mis.bad: I asked for a seat in the corridor of the plane.
mis.good: I asked for an aisle seat on the plane.
mis.why: On planes and in shops, the narrow path is an aisle, not a corridor.

def: The place in a shop where you pay for what you are buying.
ex: There was a long queue at the checkout, so we went to another shop.
nat: You can pay at the self-service checkout if you have only a few items.

mis.bad: I paid in the checkout.
mis.good: I paid at the checkout.
mis.why: Use "at" with the checkout.

def: A piece of paper or a code that you can use instead of money.
ex: I received a fifty-dollar voucher for the restaurant as a birthday gift.
nat: The hotel gave us a meal voucher because our room was not ready.

mis.bad: I paid the dinner with a voucher of gift.
mis.good: I paid for the dinner with a gift voucher.
mis.why: Use "pay for" the dinner, and the adjective-noun order "gift voucher".

def: A small piece of paper that gives you a lower price when you buy something.
ex: I used a coupon to get twenty percent off my shopping.
nat: Check your email, because the store often sends a coupon for new customers.

mis.bad: I have a coupom of discount for this store.
mis.good: I have a discount coupon for this store.
mis.why: The spelling is coupon, and the adjective noun order is "discount coupon".

def: Something that you buy, or the act of buying it.
ex: Keep the receipt as proof of purchase in case you need to return it.
nat: The company announced the purchase of two new buildings in the city center.

mis.bad: I made a purchase of a book in the internet yesterday.
mis.good: I bought a book online yesterday.
mis.why: Using the simple verb "buy" is more natural; "in the internet" should be "on the internet" or just "online".

def: Fashionable at the present time.
ex: They opened a trendy café near the station, and it is always full.
nat: I do not follow fashion, so I rarely buy trendy clothes.

mis.bad: This neighborhood is very trend and full of cafés.
mis.good: This neighborhood is very trendy and full of cafés.
mis.why: Trend is a noun; the adjective is trendy.

def: Not new; used before by another person.
ex: I bought a second-hand bike online, and it works perfectly.
nat: There is a second-hand bookshop on our street that sells cheap novels.

mis.bad: I bought a second hand car of my cousin.
mis.good: I bought a second-hand car from my cousin.
mis.why: You buy something from a person, not "of" a person, and second-hand is hyphenated before a noun.

def: A large amount of something; in bulk means in large quantities.
ex: We buy rice in bulk because it is cheaper than small packets.
nat: The bulk of our customers are students who live near the campus.

mis.bad: I bought the shampoo in bulks to save money.
mis.good: I bought the shampoo in bulk to save money.
mis.why: "In bulk" is a fixed phrase and has no plural.

def: A sudden strong wish to do something without thinking about it.
ex: I bought the shoes on impulse and later regretted the decision.
nat: She felt an impulse to call him, but she waited until the morning.

mis.bad: I bought it by impulse yesterday.
mis.good: I bought it on impulse yesterday.
mis.why: The fixed phrase is "on impulse", not "by impulse".

def: Made as a copy of something valuable in order to trick people.
ex: The police found hundreds of counterfeit watches in the small shop.
nat: Be careful with counterfeit money, because it can be very hard to spot.

mis.bad: He sold falsified perfumes in the street market.
mis.good: He sold counterfeit perfumes in the street market.
mis.why: "Falsified" is used for documents or data; fake goods are counterfeit.

def: Expensive; costing more than you would like to pay.
ex: The hotel was nice, but it was too pricey for our budget.
nat: That restaurant is a bit pricey, but the food is excellent.

mis.bad: The price of the hotel was very pricey.
mis.good: The hotel was very pricey.
mis.why: Pricey describes the thing itself, so "the price of the hotel was pricey" is repetitive.

def: A piece of paper or cloth on a product that gives information about it.
ex: Always read the label to check the ingredients before you buy food.
nat: The label inside the jacket says it must be washed by hand.

mis.bad: I read the label in the bottle.
mis.good: I read the label on the bottle.
mis.why: A label is on the surface of an object, so use "on".

def: The material that is used to wrap or protect a product.
ex: The company is trying to reduce plastic packaging to protect the environment.
nat: The packaging was damaged, but the phone inside was fine.

mis.bad: The packagings of this product are recyclable.
mis.good: The packaging of this product is recyclable.
mis.why: Packaging is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb and has no plural.

def: A person or company that delivers packages and documents.
ex: The courier delivered the package to our door before nine o'clock.
nat: We sent the contract by courier because it had to arrive today.

mis.bad: I sent the documents by a courier to the client.
mis.good: I sent the documents by courier to the client.
mis.why: After "by", transport and delivery methods take no article: by courier.

def: The goods that a shop has available to sell.
ex: Sorry, that model is out of stock, but we will get more next week.
nat: The store keeps a large stock of winter clothes in its warehouse.

mis.bad: The shoes are not in the stock now.
mis.good: The shoes are not in stock now.
mis.why: "In stock" and "out of stock" are fixed phrases without "the".

def: A name and design that make a product different from other products.
ex: This brand of coffee is more expensive, but the taste is much better.
nat: Many young people prefer well-known brands when they buy shoes.

mis.bad: I prefer the mark of this shoe.
mis.good: I prefer this brand of shoes.
mis.why: "Mark" is not used for product names; the word is brand.

def: A statement that says you are not satisfied with something.
ex: She made a complaint about the noise to the hotel manager.
nat: We received several complaints about the late delivery last week.

mis.bad: I did a complain to the manager about the service.
mis.good: I made a complaint to the manager about the service.
mis.why: "Complain" is the verb; the noun is complaint, and we "make" a complaint.

def: A set of instructions for cooking a particular dish.
ex: My grandmother gave me her recipe for chocolate cake years ago.
nat: Follow the recipe carefully if you want the sauce to taste right.

mis.bad: I looked for a recipt of the cake on the internet.
mis.good: I looked for a recipe for the cake on the internet.
mis.why: Recipe (cooking) and receipt (proof of payment) are different words; also "recipe for" is the right structure.

def: One of the foods that you use to make a dish.
ex: You only need five simple ingredients to make this soup.
nat: Fresh ingredients make a big difference to the flavor of any meal.

mis.bad: The ingredients of the recipe is very simple.
mis.good: The ingredients of the recipe are very simple.
mis.why: "Ingredients" is plural, so the verb must be "are".

def: A style of cooking that is typical of a country or region.
ex: Italian cuisine is popular all over the world, especially pasta and pizza.
nat: I love Thai cuisine, but I cannot eat very spicy food.

mis.bad: The brazilian kitchen is famous for feijoada.
mis.good: Brazilian cuisine is famous for feijoada.
mis.why: "Kitchen" is a room; the style of cooking is cuisine, and nationalities are capitalized.

def: A small dish that you eat at the beginning of a meal.
ex: We shared an appetizer of fried cheese before the main course arrived.
nat: The restaurant serves a free appetizer while you wait for your table.

mis.bad: As appetizer, we ate a salad.
mis.good: As an appetizer, we ate a salad.
mis.why: The singular countable noun needs the article "an".

def: Something sweet that you eat at the end of a meal.
ex: For dessert, we had ice cream with fresh strawberries on top.
nat: I am too full for dessert, but thank you for offering.

mis.bad: I did not eat the desert because I was full.
mis.good: I did not eat the dessert because I was full.
mis.why: Dessert (sweet food) has two s's; desert is a dry place.

def: Food that remains after a meal and can be eaten later.
ex: We ate the leftovers for lunch the next day instead of cooking.
nat: There were so many leftovers from the party that we shared them with the neighbors.

mis.bad: We have a leftovers from dinner.
mis.good: We have some leftovers from dinner.
mis.why: Leftovers is plural, so it cannot take "a".

def: To cook food over direct heat, often outside.
ex: We grilled fish and vegetables in the garden on Sunday afternoon.
nat: Do not grill the chicken for too long, or it will be dry.

mis.bad: We grilled the meat in the oven of the barbecue.
mis.good: We grilled the meat on the barbecue.
mis.why: Food is grilled "on" a barbecue, not "in the oven of".

def: To cook gently in liquid just below boiling point.
ex: Let the sauce simmer for twenty minutes, and stir it from time to time.
nat: Simmer the soup on low heat until the vegetables are soft.

mis.bad: Let the soup to simmer for ten minutes.
mis.good: Let the soup simmer for ten minutes.
mis.why: After "let" + object, use the base verb without "to".

def: To cut something into thin, flat pieces.
ex: He sliced the bread and put some cheese on each piece.
nat: Slice the tomatoes thinly so that they cook faster.

mis.bad: He sliced the bread in thin pieces of slices.
mis.good: He cut the bread into thin slices.
mis.why: Use "cut into slices"; "pieces of slices" is redundant.

def: To cut something into small pieces with a knife.
ex: She chopped the onions and garlic before adding them to the pan.
nat: Chop the herbs finely and sprinkle them over the pasta.

mis.bad: She chopped the onion in little pieces with the tip of knife.
mis.good: She chopped the onion into small pieces with the tip of the knife.
mis.why: Use "into" pieces and the article before "knife".

def: To remove the outer skin of a fruit or vegetable.
ex: I peeled the potatoes while my sister prepared the salad.
nat: It is easy to peel an orange if you start at the top.

mis.bad: She peeled the orange and eaten it.
mis.good: She peeled the orange and ate it.
mis.why: Use the simple past "ate", not the participle "eaten".

def: To move food or liquid around with a spoon.
ex: Stir the soup slowly so that it does not stick to the bottom of the pan.
nat: He stirred sugar into his coffee and looked out of the window.

mis.bad: She stir the soup every five minutes.
mis.good: She stirs the soup every five minutes.
mis.why: Third person singular present needs -s.

def: To cook food such as bread or cake in an oven.
ex: I baked a chocolate cake for my daughter's birthday party yesterday.
nat: You should bake the bread until it is golden brown.

mis.bad: I baked a cake in the stove.
mis.good: I baked a cake in the oven.
mis.why: In English, the oven bakes the food; the stove is the cooking surface on top.

def: To cook food in an oven or over a fire so that it becomes brown.
ex: We roasted a chicken with potatoes and served it with salad.
nat: Roast the vegetables at a high temperature for about forty minutes.

mis.bad: He roasts the meat in the pan with water.
mis.good: He roasts the meat in the oven without water.
mis.why: Roasting uses dry heat in an oven; cooking in water is boiling or stewing.

def: Having a strong hot flavor from spices.
ex: The curry was so spicy that I needed a glass of milk.
nat: I like spicy food, but my husband prefers mild dishes.

mis.bad: The soup is too much spicy.
mis.good: The soup is too spicy.
mis.why: Do not use "too much" before an adjective; use "too".

def: Having little taste or flavor.
ex: The soup was bland, so I added salt and some black pepper.
nat: Hospital food is often bland, but this meal was surprisingly tasty.

mis.bad: The soup tastes blandly.
mis.good: The soup tastes bland.
mis.why: After "taste", use an adjective, not an adverb.

def: The taste of a food or drink.
ex: This ice cream has a strong flavor of vanilla and caramel.
nat: What flavor of yogurt would you like, strawberry or peach?

mis.bad: The flavor of this cake is more better than that one.
mis.good: The flavor of this cake is better than that one.
mis.why: "Better" is already comparative; never say "more better".

def: The amount of food that is served to one person.
ex: The portions at this restaurant are huge, so we shared one dish.
nat: I only ate a small portion of the pasta because I was not hungry.

mis.bad: I ate two portion of rice.
mis.good: I ate two portions of rice.
mis.why: After "two" the noun must be plural.

def: Not eating meat or fish; made without meat or fish.
ex: My sister has been vegetarian for ten years and loves cooking pasta.
nat: The restaurant has a good vegetarian menu with many creative dishes.

mis.bad: I am vegetarian since two years.
mis.good: I have been vegetarian for two years.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with "for" to show duration, not the present simple with "since".

def: Not eating or using any animal products, including milk and eggs.
ex: She became vegan after watching a documentary about modern farming.
nat: This vegan cake is made without eggs, milk, or butter.

mis.bad: The vegan people eat just vegetables and fish.
mis.good: Vegan people do not eat any animal products, including fish.
mis.why: Vegans do not eat fish; the definition in the sentence is false.

def: Salt, pepper, herbs, or spices added to food to improve its taste.
ex: Add a little seasoning to the soup just before you serve it.
nat: The chef uses a special seasoning that makes the fish taste amazing.

mis.bad: I put many seasonings in the rice and it was perfect.
mis.good: I put plenty of seasoning in the rice, and it was perfect.
mis.why: Seasoning is mostly uncountable, so use "plenty of seasoning", not "many seasonings".

def: Firm and making a loud noise when you bite it.
ex: I love the crunchy crust on this bread, but the inside is soft.
nat: These crunchy carrots are delicious with a little hummus.

mis.bad: The biscuit was very croquant and tasty.
mis.good: The biscuit was very crunchy and tasty.
mis.why: "Croquant" is French; the English word is crunchy.

def: Soft and easy to cut or chew, especially meat or vegetables.
ex: The beef was so tender that it almost melted in my mouth.
nat: Cook the carrots until they are tender but not too soft.

mis.bad: The meat was so tender that was easy of chew.
mis.good: The meat was so tender that it was easy to chew.
mis.why: The result clause needs a subject ("it") and "easy to chew".

def: Ready to be picked and eaten, used for fruit.
ex: Wait until the mangoes are ripe before you cut them for dessert.
nat: These bananas are not ripe yet, so the taste is quite bitter.

mis.bad: The fruit is mature and ready to eat.
mis.good: The fruit is ripe and ready to eat.
mis.why: "Mature" is used for people, cheese, or ideas; fruit that is ready is ripe.

def: Not cooked, or not yet prepared for use.
ex: Do not eat raw eggs, because they can make you very sick.
nat: The chef served the fish raw with a little lemon and soy sauce.

mis.bad: I like my steak crude, with some blood inside.
mis.good: I like my steak rare, with some blood inside.
mis.why: "Crude" is not used for undercooked meat; steaks are rare, medium, or well done, and uncooked food is raw.

def: Any drink, usually not water, such as juice or tea.
ex: The hotel offers a free welcome beverage when guests arrive.
nat: You can bring food, but alcoholic beverages are not allowed in the park.

mis.bad: I would like a beverage cold.
mis.good: I would like a cold beverage.
mis.why: Adjectives come before the noun in English.

def: Food that you buy in a restaurant and eat somewhere else.
ex: We were too tired to cook, so we ordered a pizza takeaway.
nat: The takeaway on the corner is cheap, and the food arrives hot.

mis.bad: We ate in the takeaway because it had tables.
mis.good: We ate in the restaurant because it had tables.
mis.why: A takeaway is a place or meal you take away, so you do not eat inside it.

def: A meal where you serve yourself from a long table of food.
ex: The hotel serves a large buffet for breakfast from seven to ten.
nat: At the wedding, there was a buffet with hot and cold dishes.

mis.bad: The buffet is pronounced like in "buffalo".
mis.good: The word buffet is pronounced buh-FAY.
mis.why: The final t is silent in buffet; it does not sound like "buffalo".

def: A small extra amount of money that you give to a waiter or driver.
ex: We left a ten percent tip because the service was excellent.
nat: Do people leave a tip in restaurants in your country?

mis.bad: We left a tip to the waiter of five euros.
mis.good: We left the waiter a five-euro tip.
mis.why: Word order: we leave someone a tip; "tip to the waiter of five euros" is unnatural.

def: A man who brings food and drinks to customers in a restaurant.
ex: The waiter recommended the fish and brought us some bread.
nat: Our waiter was friendly and checked on us several times during dinner.

mis.bad: I called the waiter to bring me the account.
mis.good: I called the waiter to bring me the bill.
mis.why: In a restaurant you ask for the bill, not the "account".

def: A very strong desire for a particular food or thing.
ex: I had a craving for chocolate in the middle of the night.
nat: He ate a sandwich to satisfy his craving for something salty.

mis.bad: I have a craving of pizza right now.
mis.good: I have a craving for pizza right now.
mis.why: Craving is followed by "for", not "of".

def: A small amount of food that you eat between meals.
ex: I always take a healthy snack to work in case I get hungry.
nat: The kids ate a snack when they came home from school.

mis.bad: I snack a sandwich every afternoon.
mis.good: I have a sandwich as a snack every afternoon.
mis.why: Snack is mostly a noun in this sense; "have a snack" or "snack on" a food is the usual pattern.

def: Food and other items that you buy at a supermarket for your home.
ex: I carried the groceries up to the third floor because the elevator was broken.
nat: We do the groceries on Saturdays, when the supermarket is less crowded.

mis.bad: I went to the market to do my compras.
mis.good: I went to the supermarket to buy groceries.
mis.why: Do not use Portuguese "compras"; groceries is plural and goes with buy or do.

def: A small room or cupboard where you keep food.
ex: There is plenty of pasta and rice in the pantry if you are hungry.
nat: I need to clean the pantry because some of the food is out of date.

mis.bad: The pantry have no flour.
mis.good: The pantry has no flour.
mis.why: A singular noun takes "has".

def: The feeling that you want to eat food.
ex: I lost my appetite after hearing the bad news about my job.
nat: The long walk in the mountains gave us a big appetite.

mis.bad: I have an appetite of pizza.
mis.good: I have an appetite for pizza.
mis.why: Appetite is followed by "for", not "of".

def: A large and special meal for many people, often to celebrate something.
ex: The family prepared a huge feast for the holiday dinner.
nat: After the wedding ceremony, we had a feast with music and dancing.

mis.bad: The feast was a quick meal of only one sandwich.
mis.good: The feast was a huge meal with many dishes.
mis.why: A feast is a big meal; "a quick sandwich" cannot be a feast.

def: Made at home and not bought from a shop.
ex: My aunt brought homemade bread and a jar of strawberry jam.
nat: Nothing tastes better than a homemade pizza on a cold evening.

mis.bad: My mother made a homemaded cake.
mis.good: My mother made a homemade cake.
mis.why: Homemade is already an adjective and has no -ed ending.

def: Food prepared in a particular way, or a plate for serving it.
ex: My favorite dish is rice with beans and grilled chicken.
nat: The restaurant is famous for its traditional dishes from the north of Brazil.

mis.bad: I washed the plate yesterday, and now I will cook a new plate.
mis.good: I washed the dishes yesterday, and now I will cook a new dish.
mis.why: "Plate" is the object you eat from; "prato" as a meal is a dish.

def: To drink something slowly, taking a small amount at a time.
ex: She sipped her tea slowly and looked at the rain through the window.
nat: He sipped the hot soup carefully because he did not want to burn his tongue.

mis.bad: He sipped all the juice in one go.
mis.good: He drank all the juice in one go.
mis.why: Sip means drinking in small amounts, so "all in one go" contradicts it.

def: A sound or device that warns you about something or wakes you up.
ex: My alarm rang at six, but I turned it off and went back to sleep.
nat: The fire alarm went off, so we left the building quickly.

mis.bad: I put the alarm to ring at six.
mis.good: I set the alarm for six.
mis.why: The verb is set: "set the alarm for six".

def: A short trip to do a small job, such as buying something or posting a letter.
ex: I have a few errands to run before I come to your house.
nat: She spent the morning running errands in the city center.

mis.bad: I need to make some errands this afternoon.
mis.good: I need to run some errands this afternoon.
mis.why: The collocation is "run errands", not "make errands".

def: Clothes that need washing or have just been washed.
ex: I do the laundry every Sunday, and then I iron my shirts.
nat: There is a pile of dirty laundry in the bathroom.

mis.bad: I did the laundries and cleaned the kitchen.
mis.good: I did the laundry and cleaned the kitchen.
mis.why: Laundry is uncountable here, so it has no plural.

def: Jobs you do to keep your home clean, such as cleaning and washing.
ex: We share the housework, so nobody feels too tired at the weekend.
nat: I finish the housework before noon, and then I relax.

mis.bad: I did many houseworks this morning.
mis.good: I did a lot of housework this morning.
mis.why: Housework is uncountable, so it has no plural and cannot take "many".

def: To sleep for longer than you planned.
ex: I overslept this morning, so I missed the first bus to work.
nat: Set two alarms if you are afraid that you will oversleep.

mis.bad: I overslept the bus because I woke up late.
mis.good: I missed the bus because I overslept.
mis.why: You miss a bus; you do not "oversleep" a bus.

def: A short sleep during the day.
ex: I took a short nap after lunch and felt much better.
nat: The baby usually has a nap at about two o'clock.

mis.bad: I made a nap after lunch.
mis.good: I took a nap after lunch.
mis.why: The collocation is "take a nap" or "have a nap".

def: To let a liquid fall out of a container by accident.
ex: I spilled coffee on my shirt just before the meeting started.
nat: Be careful not to spill the milk when you pour it.

mis.bad: I poured the coffee and spilled it out of the cup accidentally on purpose.
mis.good: I poured the coffee and spilled it by accident.
mis.why: "Accidentally on purpose" contradicts itself; spill means by accident.

pt: perder (algo temporariamente), colocar no lugar errado
def: To put something somewhere and then forget where it is.
ex: I misplaced my keys this morning and searched the whole apartment.
nat: She often misplaces her phone, so she uses a tracking app.

mis.bad: I misplaced my phone, so I think someone stole it.
mis.good: I misplaced my phone, but I found it under the sofa.
mis.why: Misplace means a temporary loss by your own mistake, not theft.

def: A situation that is annoying because it causes difficulty or extra effort.
ex: Renewing my driving license was such a hassle that I almost gave up.
nat: It is no hassle at all, so please let us help you.

mis.bad: It was a big hassles to get a visa.
mis.good: It was a big hassle to get a visa.
mis.why: "A big hassle" is singular after "a".

def: The quality of being easy, useful, or suitable for your needs.
ex: Online banking is popular because of its speed and convenience.
nat: For your convenience, the shop opens at seven in the morning.

mis.bad: The shop has a convenience for the customers of parking.
mis.good: The shop offers the convenience of free parking for customers.
mis.why: Use "the convenience of + noun"; "of parking" cannot follow "customers" like that.

def: Something kind that you do to help someone.
ex: Could you do me a favor and pick up my children from school?
nat: He asked me for a favor, but I was too busy to help.

mis.bad: Can you make me a favour?
mis.good: Can you do me a favor?
mis.why: The collocation is "do someone a favor", not "make".

def: To decide that a planned event will not happen.
ex: They cancelled the concert at the last minute because the singer was sick.
nat: You can cancel your booking free of charge until Friday.

mis.bad: They canceled the meeting to the next week.
mis.good: They postponed the meeting to next week.
mis.why: Cancel means the event will not happen; to move it to another date, use postpone.

def: Slowly, over a period of time.
ex: The weather gradually became warmer and warmer as we drove further south.
nat: Gradually, she got used to living in a big city.

mis.bad: The weather gradual became warmer.
mis.good: The weather gradually became warmer.
mis.why: Use the adverb "gradually" to modify a verb.

def: In the end, especially after a long time or many problems.
ex: After three hours of waiting, we eventually got a table at the restaurant.
nat: He eventually found a job, but it took more than a year.

mis.bad: Eventually I may call you tomorrow.
mis.good: Perhaps I will call you tomorrow.
mis.why: In English eventually means "in the end", not "possibly".

def: A person you do not know.
ex: Never open the door to a stranger when your parents are not home.
nat: I felt like a stranger in my own city after ten years abroad.

mis.bad: He is a stranger from another country.
mis.good: He is a foreigner from another country.
mis.why: A stranger is someone you do not know; a person from another country is a foreigner.

def: An activity that you enjoy doing in your free time.
ex: My favorite hobby is photography, and I take my camera everywhere.
nat: He took up a new hobby after he retired, and now he paints every day.
col: turn a hobby into a job

mis.bad: My hobbie is play football.
mis.good: My hobby is playing football.
mis.why: The spelling is hobby, and after "is" use the -ing form.

def: The activity of walking long distances in nature, especially on hills or mountains.
ex: We went hiking in the mountains and stayed in a small cabin.
nat: Good hiking boots are important if you plan to walk for many hours.

mis.bad: We did hiking in the mountains last weekend.
mis.good: We went hiking in the mountains last weekend.
mis.why: Use "go hiking" for activities with -ing; "do hiking" is not natural.

def: The activity of staying outdoors in a tent for a holiday.
ex: We went camping by the lake, and the stars were beautiful at night.
nat: Camping is cheap, but you need to be ready for bad weather.

mis.bad: We went to camping near the river.
mis.good: We went camping near the river.
mis.why: After "go", camping is used without "to": go camping.

def: A place where people can put up tents and stay.
ex: The campsite has showers, a small shop, and a lovely view of the sea.
nat: We arrived at the campsite late and put up our tent in the dark.

mis.bad: We found a campsite with place to put the tent.
mis.good: We found a campsite with space to put up the tent.
mis.why: Use "space" (uncountable) for room; "place" would need an article or a different structure.

def: A path through the countryside or forest, used for walking or cycling.
ex: The trail was steep and muddy, but the view from the top was wonderful.
nat: Please stay on the trail so you do not damage the plants.

mis.bad: We walked by the trail until the top.
mis.good: We walked along the trail to the top.
mis.why: Use "along the trail" for movement on a path; "until the top" should be "to the top".

def: To lie in the sun in order to make your skin brown.
ex: We sunbathed on the beach all afternoon and forgot to put on sunscreen.
nat: You should not sunbathe in the middle of the day because the sun is too strong.

mis.bad: I like to sunbathe me on the beach.
mis.good: I like to sunbathe on the beach.
mis.why: Sunbathe is intransitive and does not take a reflexive pronoun.

def: A slow, relaxed walk, usually for pleasure.
ex: After dinner, we went for a stroll along the river.
nat: A quiet stroll in the park is a nice way to clear your mind.

mis.bad: After the dinner we did a stroll in the park.
mis.good: After dinner, we went for a stroll in the park.
mis.why: Use "go for a stroll" or "take a stroll"; also "dinner" needs no article here.

def: A meal that you eat outdoors, usually in a park or in the countryside.
ex: We had a picnic by the lake and fed the ducks.
nat: It started to rain, so we ended the picnic early.

mis.bad: We made a picnic in the park on Sunday.
mis.good: We had a picnic in the park on Sunday.
mis.why: The collocation is "have a picnic" or "go on a picnic".

def: The pleasant feeling of enjoying something funny or interesting.
ex: The children screamed with amusement when the clown fell into the water.
nat: We went to the amusement park, and the rides were great.

mis.bad: The park of amusement was closed on Monday.
mis.good: The amusement park was closed on Monday.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "amusement park", not "park of amusement".

def: A competition in which many players or teams play until there is one winner.
ex: Our team reached the final of the tournament for the first time.
nat: He won the chess tournament in his city when he was fifteen.

mis.bad: Our team played in a tournament of football in the city.
mis.good: Our team played in a football tournament in the city.
mis.why: Use the noun adjunct "football tournament", not "tournament of football".

def: A large building with seats around a field, used for sports or concerts.
ex: More than sixty thousand fans filled the stadium for the final match.
nat: The singer will perform at the national stadium next summer.

mis.bad: The match was in the stage of the city.
mis.good: The match was at the city stadium.
mis.why: "Stage" is where performers stand; a sports venue is a stadium.

def: The official who controls a game and makes sure that the rules are followed.
ex: The referee stopped the match for ten minutes because of the heavy rain.
nat: Players should not argue with the referee, even when they disagree.

mis.bad: The arbiter of the game gave a red card.
mis.good: The referee of the game gave a red card.
mis.why: "Arbiter" is not used in sports; the word is referee.

def: The winner of a competition, especially a sports competition.
ex: She became the world champion at the age of twenty-two.
nat: The champions celebrated in the streets with thousands of fans.

mis.bad: She is the champion in the tennis in the world.
mis.good: She is the world tennis champion.
mis.why: Use "world tennis champion" or "champion of the world"; the original structure is wrong.

def: A person who watches an event, especially a sports match.
ex: Thousands of spectators waited in the rain to see the final.
nat: The match was played without spectators because of safety rules.

mis.bad: The spectators of the cinema liked the film.
mis.good: The audience at the cinema liked the film.
mis.why: Spectators watch sports; for a cinema, theater, or concert use audience.

def: To make your body or a part of it longer or straighter to relax the muscles.
ex: You should always stretch your legs well before you start running.
nat: I stretched my arms above my head and yawned loudly.

mis.bad: I stretched my muscles before the run, and it was dangerous to hurt me.
mis.good: I stretched before the run so that I would not hurt myself.
mis.why: The original is not grammatical; use "so that I would not hurt myself".

pt: correr em ritmo leve, fazer jogging
def: To run slowly and steadily, usually for exercise.
ex: I jog around the park every morning before I go to work.
nat: He jogged to the bus stop because he was late.

mis.bad: I go to jog every morning near my house.
mis.good: I go jogging every morning near my house.
mis.why: After "go", use -ing: go jogging.

def: A game or problem that you solve by thinking.
ex: We spent the whole evening doing a puzzle with a thousand pieces.
nat: The mystery of the missing keys was a real puzzle to everyone.

mis.bad: I am good in puzzles.
mis.good: I am good at puzzles.
mis.why: Use "good at" for skills.

def: Time when you are not working and can do things that you enjoy.
ex: In my leisure time, I read novels and walk along the beach.
nat: The hotel has a leisure center with a pool and a gym.

mis.bad: In my times of leisure, I read many books.
mis.good: In my leisure time, I read many books.
mis.why: Say "leisure time" or "in my free time"; "times of leisure" is unnatural.

def: An activity that you do regularly for enjoyment.
ex: Cooking is his favorite pastime, and he often invites friends for dinner.
nat: Watching football is a national pastime in many countries.

mis.bad: My pastime is to be playing cards on Sundays.
mis.good: My pastime is playing cards on Sundays.
mis.why: After "is", use the simple -ing form: "playing", not "to be playing".

def: A series of events, such as music or film, or a public celebration.
ex: We camped for three days at a music festival in the countryside.
nat: The city holds a food festival every autumn, and the streets are full.

mis.bad: We went to the carnival festival in Salvador to see the parade.
mis.good: We went to the carnival in Salvador to see the parade.
mis.why: Carnival is itself a festival, so "carnival festival" is redundant.

def: The history, buildings, and traditions that a country or group has had for a long time.
ex: The old town is a World Heritage Site and attracts many visitors.
nat: We must protect our cultural heritage for future generations.

mis.bad: My heritage of my grandfather was a house.
mis.good: The inheritance from my grandfather was a house.
mis.why: Heritage is culture and history; a thing left to you is an inheritance.

def: A formal public event that is held on a special occasion.
ex: The opening ceremony of the Olympic Games was watched by millions of people.
nat: They had a small ceremony at the town hall, and then they went to a restaurant.

mis.bad: The ceremony of graduation did a lot of cry.
mis.good: The graduation ceremony made many people cry.
mis.why: Use "graduation ceremony" and "made many people cry".

def: The traditional stories, music, and beliefs of a community.
ex: Brazilian folklore includes many stories about forest spirits and magic animals.
nat: The book collects folklore from villages in the north of the country.

mis.bad: The folklores of Brazil are very rich.
mis.good: The folklore of Brazil is very rich.
mis.why: Folklore is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

def: Belonging to a time very long ago in history.
ex: We visited the ancient ruins of Rome and learned about its history.
nat: Ancient Egyptians built huge tombs for their kings.

mis.bad: The ancient building was constructed last year.
mis.good: The modern building was constructed last year.
mis.why: Ancient means very old, so it cannot describe a building made last year.

def: An object made by people in the past that is important for history.
ex: The museum has thousands of artifacts from the ancient city.
nat: Archaeologists found a rare artifact under the old church.

mis.bad: The artifact was built last week by a factory.
mis.good: The artifact was made thousands of years ago.
mis.why: An artifact is a historical object from the past, not something new.

def: A structure built to remember a famous person or event.
ex: The monument in the main square honors soldiers who died in the war.
nat: Thousands of people visit the national monument every year.

mis.bad: We went to see a monument of museum.
mis.good: We went to see a monument in the square.
mis.why: A monument is outside; "monument of museum" is a wrong structure.

def: A building or room where art is shown to the public.
ex: We spent the afternoon at an art gallery looking at modern paintings.
nat: The gallery is free on Sundays, so it is always crowded.

mis.bad: I went to the gallery of arts to see a exhibition.
mis.good: I went to the art gallery to see an exhibition.
mis.why: Use "art gallery", and "an" before exhibition.

def: A piece of art made by shaping stone, metal, or wood.
ex: The park has a huge sculpture of a horse made of metal.
nat: She makes beautiful sculptures from pieces of old wood.

mis.bad: The sculpture was painted by a famous artist.
mis.good: The sculpture was made by a famous artist.
mis.why: Sculptures are carved or shaped, not painted; paintings are painted.

def: A work of art that is the best that a person has ever produced.
ex: Many critics call this novel the masterpiece of the twentieth century.
nat: The film is a masterpiece, and I cried at the end.

mis.bad: The film is a master piece work.
mis.good: The film is a masterpiece.
mis.why: Masterpiece is one word and is already a work of art.

def: The rules of polite behavior in a society or group.
ex: Business etiquette in Japan includes giving your business card with both hands.
nat: It is bad etiquette to talk on the phone during dinner.

mis.bad: The etiquettes of the table are important.
mis.good: Table etiquette is important.
mis.why: Etiquette is uncountable and has no plural.

def: A form of a language that is spoken in a particular region.
ex: In the north of England, people speak a dialect that is hard to understand.
nat: The two villages have different dialects, even though they are close.

mis.bad: Portuguese is a dialect of Brazil.
mis.good: Brazilian Portuguese is a variety of Portuguese.
mis.why: Portuguese is a language, not a dialect; a regional form is a dialect or variety.

def: Able to speak two languages equally well.
ex: She grew up in a bilingual family and speaks both Spanish and English.
nat: Our company is looking for a bilingual assistant for the Paris office.

mis.bad: She is bilingual in three languages.
mis.good: She speaks three languages fluently.
mis.why: Bilingual means two languages; for three, say she speaks three languages.

def: A series of actions that are always done in the same way, often for a special reason.
ex: Making coffee is my morning ritual, and I never skip it.
nat: The ritual has been part of the village life for centuries.

mis.bad: My morning ritual are making coffee and reading.
mis.good: My morning ritual is making coffee and reading.
mis.why: "Ritual" is singular, so the verb is "is".

def: A song that is chosen to represent a country, team, or group.
ex: Everyone stood up when the national anthem began to play.
nat: The band wrote an anthem for the football team.

mis.bad: The hymn of Brazil is sung before the games.
mis.good: The national anthem is sung before the games.
mis.why: "Hymn" is a religious song; a country's song is its national anthem.

def: Special clothes that you wear to look like someone else or to represent a culture.
ex: The children wore bright, colorful costumes for the school party on Friday.
nat: The actors' costumes were beautiful, and the audience loved them.

mis.bad: I wore a costume of suit to the job.
mis.good: I wore a suit to work.
mis.why: A costume is for parties or the stage; clothes for work are not costumes.

def: A funny film, play, or television show.
ex: We watched a romantic comedy last night, and we laughed a lot.
nat: The theater is showing a new comedy about two neighbors.

mis.bad: The film is a comedy, so I cried of sadness.
mis.good: The film is a comedy, so I laughed a lot.
mis.why: A comedy is funny, so crying from sadness contradicts the meaning.

def: A story or film that is exciting because it has danger and mystery.
ex: I stayed awake all night reading a thriller about a stolen painting.
nat: The new thriller is so tense that I could not look at the screen.

mis.bad: The thriller was so relaxing that I fell asleep.
mis.good: The thriller was so tense that I could not look away.
mis.why: A thriller is exciting and tense, so "relaxing" contradicts its meaning.

def: One part of a television or radio series.
ex: I watched three episodes of the series before going to bed.
nat: The final episode of the season will be shown on Sunday.

mis.bad: I watched two episode of the series last night.
mis.good: I watched two episodes of the series last night.
mis.why: After "two" the noun must be plural.

def: A short video that shows parts of a film to make people want to see it.
ex: The trailer looked great, so we bought tickets for the opening night.
nat: I saw the trailer on social media, and I immediately wanted to watch the film.

mis.bad: I saw a trailer of the movie after I watched it, to know what happens.
mis.good: I saw the trailer before the movie to find out what it was about.
mis.why: A trailer is a preview, so you watch it before the film, not after.

def: Information that tells you what happens in a story before you read or watch it.
ex: Please do not give me any spoilers, because I have not finished the series.
nat: The review contains spoilers, so do not read it before the film.

mis.bad: Do not spoil me the end of the film.
mis.good: Do not spoil the end of the film for me.
mis.why: Spoil takes the thing as a direct object, and the person comes after "for".

def: The words of a song.
ex: I know the melody, but I do not remember the lyrics.
nat: The lyrics of this song are about love and distance.

mis.bad: I learned the letter of this song by heart.
mis.good: I learned the lyrics of this song by heart.
mis.why: "Letter" is a message; the words of a song are lyrics.

def: A public performance of music by singers or musicians.
ex: We bought tickets to a rock concert, and the band was fantastic.
nat: The concert starts at eight, but the doors open at seven.

mis.bad: I assisted a concert last night.
mis.good: I went to a concert last night.
mis.why: "Assist" means help; "attend" or "go to" is the right verb for an event.

def: A person who entertains an audience, such as a singer, dancer, or actor.
ex: The street performer attracted a large crowd with his magic tricks.
nat: She is a talented performer who can sing, dance, and act.

mis.bad: The performer entertained the audience with a cooking exam.
mis.good: The performer entertained the audience with a magic show.
mis.why: Performers entertain with shows, not exams.

def: The sound of many people clapping their hands to show that they enjoyed something.
ex: The audience gave her a long round of applause at the end.
nat: There was loud applause when the winner walked onto the stage.

mis.bad: The audience gave many applauses to the actor.
mis.good: The audience gave the actor a lot of applause.
mis.why: Applause is uncountable; there is no plural.

def: A practice of a play, concert, or performance before the real one.
ex: We have a rehearsal on Friday, and the show opens on Saturday.
nat: The band had three rehearsals this week to prepare for the concert.

mis.bad: We made a rehearsal of the play yesterday.
mis.good: We had a rehearsal for the play yesterday.
mis.why: Use "have a rehearsal"; "make" is not the right verb.

def: The written text of a film, including the words that the actors say.
ex: He wrote the screenplay in six months and sent it to a producer.
nat: The film won an award for the best screenplay.

mis.bad: He wrote the screenplay of the book in a novel.
mis.good: He adapted the novel into a screenplay.
mis.why: A screenplay is for a film; "adapt A into B" is the right structure.

def: A long written story about imaginary people and events.
ex: I just finished a historical novel set in Rio at the beginning of the twentieth century.
nat: She wrote her first novel at the age of twenty.

mis.bad: I read a romance of Machado de Assis.
mis.good: I read a novel by Machado de Assis.
mis.why: "Romance" in English means a love story; a long book is a novel, and the author comes after "by".

def: A person who writes books or articles.
ex: The author signed copies of her new book at the festival.
nat: Who is your favorite author, and what is the best book you have read?

mis.bad: The author of this book are very famous.
mis.good: The author of this book is very famous.
mis.why: The subject is "the author" (singular), so use "is".

def: A book that sells very many copies.
ex: Her first novel became an international bestseller within a few months.
nat: I do not usually read bestsellers, because I prefer smaller books.

mis.bad: She is a bestseller author.
mis.good: She is a bestselling author.
mis.why: The adjective is "bestselling"; a bestseller is the book itself.

def: A recorded program that you can download or listen to online.
ex: I listen to a podcast about history while I wash the dishes.
nat: The podcast has more than a million listeners every week.

mis.bad: I assist to a podcast every morning.
mis.good: I listen to a podcast every morning.
mis.why: "Assist" means help; use "listen to" for audio.

def: A person who prepares a newspaper, book, or film for publication.
ex: The editor of the newspaper read the story and asked for changes.
nat: My editor said the article was too long and cut two paragraphs.

mis.bad: I am working as an editor in a newspaper since 2020.
mis.good: I have been working as an editor at a newspaper since 2020.
mis.why: Use the present perfect continuous with "since", and "at" a company.

def: The reporting of news about an event or subject.
ex: The live television coverage of the election lasted for the whole night.
nat: The newspaper gave the story a lot of coverage.

mis.bad: The coverages of the news are very good.
mis.good: The news coverage is very good.
mis.why: Coverage is uncountable and has no plural.

def: A newspaper with small pages that has short stories, many photos, and often gossip.
ex: The tabloid published a photo of the singer on the front page.
nat: I do not trust tabloids, because they often exaggerate the news.

mis.bad: The tabloid is a serious newspaper with deep analysis.
mis.good: The tabloid is a popular newspaper with short stories and photos.
mis.why: Tabloids are known for gossip, not deep analysis.

def: A notice or short film that tries to persuade people to buy something.
ex: I saw an advertisement for a new phone on the bus.
nat: Companies spend a lot of money on advertisements during football matches.

mis.bad: I saw a propaganda of a new phone on the bus.
mis.good: I saw an advertisement for a new phone on the bus.
mis.why: "Propaganda" in English means political persuasion; commercial ads are advertisements.

pt: exagerar, fazer algo em excesso (ex.: maratonar)
def: To do something, such as watching shows or eating, too much in a short time.
ex: We binged an entire series last weekend and barely left the sofa.
nat: It is easy to binge on snacks when you feel stressed.

mis.bad: We binged for watching the series all night.
mis.good: We binged on the series all night.
mis.why: After binge, use "on" + noun, or the compound binge-watch.

def: Having beautiful views of nature.
ex: We took the scenic route along the coast instead of the motorway.
nat: The train ride through the mountains is one of the most scenic in Europe.

mis.bad: The road was very scenery and we stopped many times.
mis.good: The road was very scenic, and we stopped many times.
mis.why: Scenery is a noun; the adjective is scenic.

pt: sala de espera, sala de estar
def: A comfortable room in a hotel, airport, or home where people can relax.
ex: We waited in the airport lounge until the gate number appeared on the screen.
nat: The hotel has a quiet lounge with sofas and a small bar.

mis.bad: We waited in the lounge of the plane.
mis.good: We waited in the airport lounge.
mis.why: A lounge is a room in a building, not inside a plane.

pt: filme de grande sucesso de bilheteria
def: A very popular film that earns a lot of money.
ex: The new superhero film became a summer blockbuster and earned millions in a week.
nat: I prefer quiet dramas to big blockbusters with loud explosions.

mis.bad: The film was a blockbuster, so nobody went to see it.
mis.good: The film was a blockbuster, so everyone went to see it.
mis.why: A blockbuster is very popular, so "nobody went" contradicts the meaning.

def: Friendly and generous treatment of guests or visitors.
ex: The family welcomed us with great hospitality and cooked a huge dinner.
nat: She works in the hospitality industry, mainly in hotels and restaurants.

mis.bad: Thank you for the hospital of your house.
mis.good: Thank you for your hospitality.
mis.why: "Hospital" is where sick people go; the word for welcoming guests is hospitality.

def: A large case with a handle that you use to carry your clothes when you travel.
ex: I packed my suitcase the night before, so I was calm in the morning.
nat: The wheel of my suitcase broke at the airport, so I had to carry it.

mis.bad: I put my clothes in the valise and closed it.
mis.good: I put my clothes in the suitcase and closed it.
mis.why: "Valise" is a rare, old-fashioned word; suitcase is the normal word.

def: A building at an airport or station where passengers begin or end a journey.
ex: Our flight leaves from Terminal Two, so we should take the free shuttle.
nat: The bus terminal was crowded with people returning home after the holiday.

mis.bad: We arrived at the terminal of the airplane.
mis.good: We arrived at the airport terminal.
mis.why: A terminal belongs to an airport or station, not to a plane.

def: The large entrance area inside a hotel or public building.
ex: We agreed to meet in the hotel lobby at nine o'clock.
nat: There are sofas and a small café in the lobby of the building.

mis.bad: I will wait for you in the lobbie.
mis.good: I will wait for you in the lobby.
mis.why: The spelling is lobby, and the plural is lobbies.

def: A kitchen machine that keeps food cold.
ex: There is no milk in the fridge, so I have to go to the shop.
nat: Please put the leftovers in the fridge after dinner.

mis.bad: I keep the milk inside the freezer to be cold.
mis.good: I keep the milk in the fridge to keep it cold.
mis.why: A freezer makes things frozen; the fridge keeps them cold.

def: A kitchen machine that heats food very quickly using waves of energy.
ex: I heated the soup in the microwave for two minutes.
nat: You should not put metal plates in the microwave because it is dangerous.

mis.bad: I heated the soup in the micro-waves oven.
mis.good: I heated the soup in the microwave.
mis.why: It is one word, "microwave", and the oven part is optional and not plural.

def: A shop where bread and cakes are made and sold.
ex: I buy fresh bread from the bakery on the corner every morning.
nat: The smell from the bakery made me hungry as I walked past.

mis.bad: I buy bread at the bakeria near my house.
mis.good: I buy bread at the bakery near my house.
mis.why: The correct spelling is bakery.

def: A person or company that sells things, often outside or in a market.
ex: A street vendor sold us hot corn and cold drinks near the beach.
nat: The vendor gave me a discount because I bought three bags.

mis.bad: The vendor of the supermarket helped me.
mis.good: The assistant at the supermarket helped me.
mis.why: A vendor sells in a market or on the street; staff in a shop are assistants.

def: The first public showing of a film, play, or show.
ex: The actors walked on the red carpet at the premiere of the film.
nat: The play had its premiere in London before it came to New York.

mis.bad: The premiere of the film is the last day of the festival after it.
mis.good: The premiere of the film is on the first day of the festival.
mis.why: A premiere is the first showing, so it cannot be the last.

def: A funny television series about a group of characters in everyday situations.
ex: We watched an old sitcom and laughed at the same jokes again.
nat: My favorite sitcom is about six friends who live in New York.

mis.bad: The sitcom is a serious drama about war.
mis.good: The sitcom is a funny series about family life.
mis.why: A sitcom is a comedy, not a serious drama.
